content.user_title: Research Conditional Answers Through Theory and History
content.value_statement: Complex questions often receive unsupported theories or misleading historical comparisons. This skill combines theory checks, structural case comparisons, and counterexamples to develop answers with clear conditions.
actual_capabilities: Review claims for overgeneralization, causal leaps, definition changes, and unsupported inferences.
Map relevant fields, authors, and theories, then rank candidates by mechanism fit, source reliability, and clear boundaries.
Build structural fingerprints using roles, stages, scarce resources, constraints, and desired changes.
Compare historical successes, failures, cross-domain examples, and counterexamples through a structured analogy matrix.
Distinguish mature consensus, conditional answers, and unresolved questions while marking evidence status and failure boundaries.
Develop audience problem maps and short-video outlines that connect theoretical mechanisms to observable actions.
limitations: This package contains instructions and interface metadata, not an executable research engine or bundled historical database.
Source verification depends on supplied materials and available research tools; uncertain facts must remain labeled.
Historical similarities do not establish causation or guarantee that past methods will work today.
Chinese translation and naming conventions shape the default output; theory-only citation support falls outside the stated activation scope.

use_cases.title: Evaluate a strategic constraint
use_cases.description: Compare a team's delivery bottleneck with relevant theories and historical transitions, then identify conditions for a workable response.

use_cases.title: Develop evidence-based teaching material
use_cases.description: Connect a theory to concrete audience problems, examine historical examples, and produce short-video outlines with observable actions.

use_cases.title: Test a proposed explanation
use_cases.description: Assess a causal claim using source checks, structural case comparisons, failures, and counterexamples before presenting a qualified conclusion.

prompt_templates.title: Explore a practical question
prompt_templates.prompt: Use dbs-standard-answer to explain why teams struggle to balance delivery and learning. Give a direct answer, relevant theory, historical comparisons, and clear limits.

prompt_templates.title: Review a claim
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this claim: [claim]. Identify overgeneralizations, select relevant theories, compare historical successes and failures, and label unverified evidence. State when the claim holds.

prompt_templates.title: Turn research into a teaching outline
prompt_templates.prompt: Study [theory] for [audience]. Check its meaning and sources, map practical problems, and compare historical cases. Produce three short-video outlines with actions and verification.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: connect theory research to teaching content.

prompt_templates.title: Conduct a bounded comparative study
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze [decision] under [constraints] using only [materials], without browsing. Build a structural fingerprint, theory map, and analogy matrix. Assess failures, counterexamples, evidence gaps, and conditions.
prompt_templates.scenario: Expert: synthesize evidence under explicit research constraints.

output_examples.input: Must a successful founder stop delivering client work to build an organization? Use only the information in this question.
output: Direct answer: No universal rule follows from this question. Delivery and capability building compete for time, but delegation depends on task repeatability and resources.
Theory research: Treat resource allocation and organizational learning as candidate lenses. No specific theory source has been verified.
Historical comparison: No cases were supplied or verified. Search for both successful delegation and failures under similar constraints before drawing historical conclusions.
Conclusion: This is a provisional hypothesis, not a historically established answer. Track delivery quality and founder workload during a limited delegation test.

output_examples.input: Create a short-video direction about using theory to solve audience problems. Include historical comparison, but do not invent evidence.
output: Direct answer: Start with a specific audience problem, explain one mechanism, and offer an action whose result can be observed.
Theory research: Check whether a learning theory actually explains the proposed change. Label any source that has not been verified.
Historical comparison: Compare documented teaching successes with unsuccessful transfers. Evidence is still needed before claiming a repeated historical mechanism.
Video outline: Open with a common mistake, demonstrate one correction, and ask viewers to compare results. Present the approach as a test, not a guarantee.

best_practices: State the problem, constraints, desired result, and permitted research scope before requesting analysis.
Request source status, competing explanations, failure cases, and counterexamples alongside supporting evidence.
Use conclusions only within their stated conditions and validate proposed actions against observable results.
anti_patterns: Treating one famous story or quotation as proof of a universal solution.
Matching cases by industry or personal identity while ignoring constraints and causal mechanisms.
Presenting unverified quotations, inferred motives, or historical analogies as established facts.

faq.question: What does standard answer mean here?
faq.answer: It means a mechanism supported by credible theory or independent cases, with explicit conditions and limits. The result may remain unresolved.

faq.question: Do I need to provide a theory first?
faq.answer: No. The workflow starts from your question and proposes relevant mechanisms and theories while clearly labeling assumptions.

faq.question: Does the skill always browse the web?
faq.answer: No. It permits browsing only when external facts materially affect the answer or verification is requested. It explicitly respects requests not to browse.

faq.question: How does it handle missing evidence?
faq.answer: It marks unverified claims, explains missing case categories, and reduces conclusion strength. Repeated verification failures should end the search for that fact.

faq.question: Can it help create videos or courses?
faq.answer: Yes. It can add requested teaching formats after research. Video outlines connect audience problems, mechanisms, practical actions, demonstrations, and observable results.

faq.question: Does it execute scripts or install dependencies?
faq.answer: The reviewed package contains only research instructions and interface metadata. Its backticks format Markdown; it supplies no executable scripts or installation steps.
